name: Colic in babies: what it is and what helps
summary: The NHS describes colic as a baby crying a lot with no obvious cause, which it says usually gets better by around 3 or 4 months, with comfort methods to try.
keyPoints: The NHS says colic is a common problem in which a baby cries a lot for no obvious reason.
The NHS lists clenched fists, a red face and drawn-up knees among the signs, with crying often worse in the afternoon and evening.
The NHS says holding, winding, gentle rocking, a warm bath and white noise may help, and that there is no cure.
The NHS says anti-colic drops and herbal or probiotic supplements are not recommended because there is no evidence they help.
The NHS advises calling NHS 111 or seeing a GP if parents are worried, and going to A&E or calling 999 for a weak or high-pitched cry.

body.heading: What is colic in babies?
body.body: The NHS says colic is when a baby cries a lot and there is no obvious cause. It describes colic as a common problem. NHS Inform describes a baby with colic as healthy but crying often and excessively, and hard to soothe. The main NHS colic page describes crying for more than 3 hours a day, on 3 days a week, for at least a week. An NHS Best Start page gives a pattern that has lasted 3 weeks or more, so the exact wording differs between pages. Local NHS leaflets say crying in young babies typically peaks when a baby is around 4 to 8 weeks old.

body.heading: What are the signs of colic?
body.body: The NHS says a baby with colic is often hard to settle. A baby may clench their fists, go red in the face or draw their knees up. The NHS says crying may happen more often in the afternoon and evening.

body.heading: What causes colic?
body.body: The NHS says there is no known reason why some babies get colic. Explanations it mentions include babies finding food harder to digest when they are very young, and food allergies such as cow's milk allergy. NHS Inform says one possible cause is trapped wind causing stomach pain. The NHS says colic can affect babies whether they are breastfed or bottle fed. These are possible explanations, not proven causes.

body.heading: What may help a baby with colic?
body.body: The NHS says there is no actual cure for colic, only ways to give relief and soothe a baby. Suggestions on its colic page include holding or cuddling the baby, gentle rocking, a warm bath and gentle white noise. It also suggests holding a baby upright during feeds so they swallow less air, and winding them after feeds. For bottle feeding, the NHS says to keep the baby as upright as possible and make sure milk fills the teat so there are no air pockets. It adds that some parents use a fast-flow teat, which may help a baby swallow less air. The NHS says an anti-colic bottle may be worth trying. A Frimley NHS page adds that if a baby finishes a feed in less than 20 minutes, the hole in the teat might be too large. A Hampshire NHS page advises never forcing a baby to take the whole feed. On breastfeeding, the NHS says a parent does not need to change their own diet as a first step.

body.heading: What is not proven to help?
body.body: The NHS says remedies such as anti-colic drops, and herbal or probiotic supplements, are not recommended. It states there is no evidence that they help colic. NHS Dumfries and Galloway, citing NICE clinical knowledge summaries, says simeticone and lactase drops should not be recommended because the evidence is not enough. Local NHS pathways differ on drops, and a Hampshire NHS page says there is no evidence that anti-colic milks bring extra benefit. MedlinePlus, a US source, mentions simethicone drops for gas and suggests asking a pharmacist or health visitor first.

body.heading: When does colic get better, and when should parents seek advice?
body.body: The NHS says colic should get better by around 3 or 4 months of age. Another NHS page says it usually stops on its own by around 6 months. The NHS advises calling NHS 111 or seeing a GP if a parent is worried, if nothing seems to work, if coping is hard, or if the baby is not gaining weight as expected. It gives the same route if symptoms continue after 4 months. The NHS says to go to A&E or call 999 if a baby has a weak or high-pitched cry, or a cry that does not sound like their normal cry. MedlinePlus lists a sudden change in crying, fever, forceful vomiting, diarrhoea or bloody stools as reasons to contact a health provider right away.

body.heading: Where can parents get support?
body.body: Local NHS programmes say infant crying is normal, comforting methods can help, and it is fine to walk away for a few minutes. They say this is when a baby is safe and the parent needs to feel calmer. They also say never to shake a baby, because shaking can cause brain damage. If a parent feels they may shake or hurt their baby, the NHS says to get help straight away. Cry-sis is a charity for parents with unsettled babies, and one NHS page lists its helpline as 0800 448 0737, open 9am to 10pm every day. A GP or health visitor can also be asked for help.
